དངོས་པོ་དང་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པར་ལྟ་བ་དེ་དག་སྤང་བར་བྱའོ། །ཡང་གཞན་ཡང་། གལ་ཏེ་རང་གཞན་#ཡོད་ཉིད་ན། །དེ་ནི་མེད་ཉིད་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །རང་བཞིན་གཞན་དུ་འགྱུར་བ་ནི། །ནམ་ཡང་འཐད་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །གལ་ཏེ་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་ཡོད་པ་ཉིད་ཡིན་ན། དེ་ལྟ་ན་དེ་ནི་མེད་པ་
ཉིད་དུ་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། རང་བཞིན་གཞན་དུ་འགྱུར་བ་ནི་ནམ་ཡང་འཐད་པར་མི་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཡང་གཞན་ཡང་། རང་བཞིན་ཡོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ན། །གཞན་དུ་འགྱུར་བ་གང་གི་ཡིན། །རང་བཞིན་ཡོད་པ་ཡིན་ན་ཡང་། །གཞན་དུ་འགྱུར་བ་#ཇི་ལྟར་རུང་། །

བ་#རྟག་པར་འཛིན། །མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ཆད་པར་ལྟ། །དེ་ཕྱིར་ཡོད་དང་མེད་པ་ལ། །མཁས་པས་གནས་པར་མི་བྱའོ#། །ཡོད་ཅེས་བྱ་བར་#དེ་ལྟར་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་ན་རྟག་པར་འཛིན་པ་ཡིན་ལ། མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ལྟར་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་ན་ཆད་པར་ལྟ་བ་ཡིན་པས། དེ་#ཕྱིར་ཡོད་པ་

ཞིག་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ཡོད་པ་དེ་ནི་ཕྱིས་མེད་པ་ཉིད་དུ་མི་འཐད་དེ། རང་བཞིན་ནི་མི་འགྱུར་བས་དེའི་ཕྱིར་ཡོད་པ་ཉིད་དུ་ལྟ་བ་ལས་རྟག་པར་ལྟ་བར་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དངོས་པོ་དེ་སྔོན་བྱུང་བ་དེ་ལྟར་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་དངོས་པོ་ཡོད་པ་ལ་འཇིག་པར་ལྟ་བ་དེས་ན་ཆད་པར་ལྟ་བར་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་

Views such as existence and non-existence must be abandoned. Furthermore:

If inherent existence or other-existence existed,
Then non-existence would not occur.
The change of an inherent nature
Is never feasible.

If a thing existed by its own inherent nature, then it would not become non-existent. Why? Because the change of an inherent nature <note>original: <term>svabhāva</term></note> is never feasible. Furthermore:

If inherent nature does not exist,
To what does change belong?
Even if inherent nature did exist,
How could change be appropriate?

If the existence of things does not exist by inherent nature, then to what would that change belong? Even if things existed by inherent nature, how could it be appropriate for that very thing to change? That is also not feasible. Furthermore:

"It exists" is a grasp for permanence;
"It does not exist" is a view of nihilism.
Therefore, regarding existence and non-existence,
The wise should not remain.

If one is thus obsessed with "it exists," it is a grasp for permanence. If one is thus obsessed with "it does not exist," it is a view of nihilism. Therefore, the wise should not remain in either existence or non-existence. Here it is asked: "How does it follow that these are views of permanence and nihilism?" Here it is explained:

Whatever exists by its own essence
Is permanent, as it is not non-existent.
"It existed before but now does not,"
That results in a view of nihilism.

Whatever exists by its own essence <note>original: <term>svabhāva</term></note> is not feasible to become non-existent later, because inherent nature does not change. Therefore, from the view of existence, it follows that one has a view of permanence. To view a thing that previously existed as no longer existing—viewing a thing that exists as being destroyed—results in the consequence of a view of nihilism. Thus, because many faults arise from viewing things as having existence or non-existence, the statement that things lack inherent nature is the vision of reality. This is the Middle Way, and it is the establishment of the ultimate truth.

This concludes the examination of existence and non-existence,
old_translation:
Furthermore:
If inherent nature does not exist,
To whom does change belong?
Even if inherent nature did exist,
How could change be appropriate?
If the existence of entities did not have an inherent nature, to whom would change belong? Even if they did have an inherent nature, how could it be appropriate for that very thing to change? That too would not be logical.

Furthermore:
To say "it is" is a grasp at permanence;
To say "it is not" is a view of nihilism.
Therefore, regarding "is" and "is not,"
The wise should not abide in either.
To obsessively cling to "it is" is the grasp at permanence. To obsessively cling to "it is not" is the view of nihilism. Therefore, the wise should not abide in either existence or non-existence.

It is said here: How does it result in the faults of the views of permanence and nihilism?

To this, it is explained:
Since that which exists by inherent nature
Does not become non-existent, it is permanent.
To say "what existed before is now no more"
Results in a view of nihilism.
That which exists by inherent nature cannot logically become non-existent later, because nature does not change; thus, the view of existence leads to the fault of a view of permanence. To look at an existing entity and see its destruction, saying "that which existed before no longer exists," leads to the fault of a view of nihilism.

Thus, because viewing entities as either existent or non-existent leads to many faults, the statement that "entities lack inherent nature" is the vision of reality. This is the Middle Way, and it is the establishment of the ultimate truth.

This is called the Examination of Existence and Non-existence, the fifteenth chapter.

<summary>This page concludes the fifteenth chapter by showing how views of existence and non-existence lead to the extremes of permanence and nihilism. It identifies the lack of inherent nature as the Middle Way and ultimate truth.</summary>
<keywords>inherent nature, change, permanence, nihilism, existence, non-existence, Middle Way, ultimate truth, Examination of Existence and Non-existence</keywords>
